lead: This unit shows how a changing inductance or capacitance becomes a usable measurement signal. After it you can explain an LVDT, an eddy current probe and a capacitive pressure sensor, and calculate their output for a given displacement or pressure.
about: The unit moves from magnetic-field sensing to electric-field sensing. Chapter 3.1 gives self and mutual inductance and variable reluctance, the base of every inductive transducer. Chapter 3.2 builds the LVDT from that base for displacement and thickness. Chapter 3.3 extends mutual inductance to rotary devices: induction potentiometer, synchros and microsyn. Chapter 3.4 adds eddy current transducers, and 3.5 turns them into proximity switches. The second half starts at 3.6 with capacitive types and signal conditioning, then 3.7 applies the variable-gap capacitor to microphones and pressure sensors. Construction, characteristics, applications and numerical output calculations run through all chapters.

chapters.idea: A coil's inductance depends on the magnetic reluctance of its path, so a small mechanical movement that changes an air gap changes inductance and can be measured.
chapters.depth: Cover self inductance L = N²/R and mutual inductance M = k√(L₁L₂), where N is the number of turns, R is reluctance, and k is the coupling coefficient. Explain magnetic reluctance R = l/(μA); for an air gap R = g/(μ₀A), where g is gap length, μ₀ is free-space permeability and A is area. Show the single-coil variable reluctance type and the two-coil mutual inductance type. Construction: iron core, armature, coil and air gap. Characteristics: output is nonlinear because L ∝ 1/g in a simple gap, sensitivity falls as gap rises, and AC excitation is needed. Applications: displacement, thickness, and pressure through a diaphragm. Some syllabi call these variable reluctance transducers or inductive transducers.

figure.title: Variable reluctance transducer
figure.aria: Block diagram of a variable reluctance transducer: AC excitation sets a coil field, the armature gap sets reluctance, and inductance changes the bridge output.

chapters.example: A variable reluctance displacement sensor has N = 500 turns, core area A = 2 × 10⁻⁴ m², nominal air gap g = 1.0 mm, and μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m. Find the inductance at 1.0 mm and at 1.2 mm, and the percentage change.
chapters.trap: Treating L as linear in gap. L ∝ 1/g, so a 20% gap rise gives about a 16.7% fall, not 20%. Also a DC ohmmeter cannot measure inductance.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: sensitivity, linearity and calibration; basic magnetic circuits (reluctance and Faraday's law) from physics.
chapters.leave: AC bridge circuits and demodulators to Unit 6; LVDT construction to 3.2; eddy current effects to 3.4.

chapters.idea: An LVDT converts core displacement into a differential AC voltage whose magnitude gives distance and whose phase gives direction.
chapters.depth: Construction: primary winding at the centre, two identical secondary windings placed symmetrically, a movable high-permeability core, an insulating former and a shield. Principle: primary AC excitation induces voltages V₁ and V₂; at the null position the core is centred and V₁ = V₂, so the differential output is zero. Off null, V_out = V₁ − V₂; magnitude is proportional to displacement over the linear range, and phase reverses across the null. Characteristics: linearity, sensitivity in mV/mm per volt of excitation, residual voltage, range, null repeatability and need for phase-sensitive demodulation. Applications: displacement, thickness, pressure through a Bourdon tube or diaphragm, and position feedback. Some syllabi call it a linear variable differential transformer.

figure.title: LVDT signal path
figure.aria: Block diagram of an LVDT: primary excitation induces two secondary voltages, core displacement changes their coupling, and the differential output is demodulated.

chapters.example: An LVDT is excited at 5 V rms. At a core position the secondary voltages are V₁ = 2.00 V rms and V₂ = 1.60 V rms. The sensitivity is 0.50 V/mm. Find the differential output, the displacement and the direction. What is the output at the null position?
chapters.trap: Taking the AC output magnitude alone as displacement. Phase reverses at null, so a simple voltmeter gives the same reading on either side. Also V_out is not proportional beyond the linear range, and residual null voltage is not zero.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 mutual inductance and variable reluctance; Unit 1 linearity and sensitivity.
chapters.leave: Demodulator and bridge circuits to Unit 6; pressure sensor construction to 3.7.

chapters.idea: Rotary inductive devices produce a voltage set by shaft angle, using mutual inductance between stator and rotor windings.
chapters.depth: Induction potentiometer: a rotary variable transformer with a distributed winding; output amplitude varies with rotor angle, giving an angle-to-voltage device. Synchro: a transmitter and a control transformer; the transmitter has a three-phase stator and a single-phase rotor, its output amplitude and phase relate to angle, and the control transformer output is approximately E_max sin(Δθ) near null; used for servo error detection. Microsyn: a compact, high-sensitivity inductive angle or rate device with a toothed rotor and stator, used in gyros and instruments. Characteristics: linearity over a limited angle, null voltage, excitation frequency and phase. Applications: radar antenna position, valve position and servo systems. Keep microsyn construction brief; only a few universities ask for its full magnetic design.

figure.aria: Tree of rotary inductive devices: induction potentiometer, synchro with transmitter and control transformer, and microsyn.

chapters.example: A synchro transmitter rotor is at θ_T = 30°. The control transformer rotor is at θ_R = 40°. The excitation is 26 V rms and the control transformer output at 90° error is 10 V rms. Find the error angle and the control transformer output. Which way should the servo turn?
chapters.trap: Assuming output is proportional to Δθ itself. A synchro control transformer gives E_max sin Δθ; sin 10° is 0.174, not 0.10. Also transmitter and control transformer are not interchangeable.
chapters.leave: AC servo motors and gear trains to Unit 6; three-phase machine theory to electrical machines.

chapters.idea: A changing magnetic field from a coil induces eddy currents in a nearby conductor, and the resulting coil impedance change measures gap, conductivity or defects without contact.
chapters.depth: Principle: an AC-excited coil creates an alternating field; a conductive target carries eddy currents; their field opposes the coil field; coil impedance (inductance and resistance) changes. Lift-off (gap between probe and target), target conductivity and permeability set the change. Construction: coil in a probe, oscillator, bridge and demodulator. Characteristics: short range of the order of the coil diameter, sensitive to target material, works in dirty environments, and uses high excitation frequency. Applications: displacement, vibration, thickness, crack detection, conductivity sorting and proximity. Some syllabi call these eddy current sensors or eddy current proximity probes.

figure.title: Eddy current measurement
figure.aria: Block diagram: an oscillator drives a probe coil, eddy currents in the target change coil impedance, and a bridge plus demodulator gives an output.

chapters.example: An eddy current displacement sensor has a linear calibration: at gap 1.0 mm its output is 6.0 V, and sensitivity is −2.5 V/mm (output falls as gap increases). Find the output at 2.2 mm and the gap when the output is 4.5 V.
chapters.trap: Using the calibration for a different target metal. Aluminium, brass and steel give different outputs at the same gap; also the sensor has a small linear range, not from zero to infinity.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 inductance and magnetic reluctance; Unit 1 calibration.
chapters.leave: Oscillator, bridge and demodulator circuits to Unit 6; ON/OFF proximity switching to 3.5; non-destructive testing detail to a later course.

chapters.idea: A proximity sensor turns a short-range physical change into a clean ON/OFF signal when a target enters its sensing field.
chapters.depth: Focus on inductive and capacitive types. Inductive: an oscillator drives a coil field, a target enters, eddy current loss reduces the field amplitude, and a threshold detector switches. Capacitive: an electrode and the target form a capacitor; the target changes capacitance and a threshold circuit switches. Define rated sensing distance S_n (specified for a mild-steel target), correction factor for other metals, hysteresis, repeatability, flush and non-flush mounting, NPN/PNP output, and normally open/normally closed contacts. Measurement uses: counting parts, detecting end of stroke, safety guards and level detection. Some syllabi call these proximity switches.

figure.title: Inductive proximity sensor
figure.aria: Block diagram of an inductive proximity sensor: oscillator field, target entry, field loss, threshold detector and ON/OFF output.

chapters.example: An inductive proximity sensor has rated sensing distance S_n = 8 mm for a mild-steel target. Its correction factor for brass is 0.80 and for stainless steel 0.70. A brass target is 7.0 mm away. Will the sensor detect it? What is the maximum brass distance? What about stainless steel at 6.0 mm?
chapters.trap: Using S_n as the distance for every metal. S_n is specified for a standard mild-steel target; correction factors reduce it. Also ignore hysteresis: the release distance is larger than the operate distance.
chapters.prereq: 3.4 eddy current effect for the inductive type; Unit 1 threshold and calibration.
chapters.leave: Capacitive field theory to 3.6; optical and Hall proximity sensors to Unit 4; PLC wiring to a practical lab.

chapters.idea: A capacitor changes with plate gap, area or dielectric, and a signal-conditioning circuit converts that small capacitance change into a usable voltage.
chapters.depth: Types: variable gap (pressure, microphone), variable area (displacement), and variable dielectric (level, thickness). Formula C = ε₀εrA/d, where ε₀ is free-space permittivity, εr is relative permittivity, A is plate area and d is gap. Construction: parallel plates, diaphragm, guard ring and shielding. Characteristics: high resolution, low force, good for small displacements, but nonlinear for gap and sensitive to stray capacitance and temperature. Signal conditioning: AC bridge or capacitance-to-voltage converter, excitation, amplifier, demodulator, filter and linearisation; guard drive and shielded cable. Applications: displacement, pressure, level, humidity and touch. Some syllabi call this a capacitance transducer.

figure.title: Capacitive transducer signal path
figure.aria: Block diagram: a change in gap, area or dielectric changes capacitance, an AC bridge converts it to voltage, and amplifier plus demodulator give the output.

chapters.example: A parallel-plate capacitive displacement sensor has plate area A = 100 mm², air gap d = 0.50 mm, and air εr = 1. Use ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m. Find C. If the gap falls to 0.40 mm, find the new C and the percentage change.
chapters.trap: Assuming C changes linearly with gap. C ∝ 1/d, so a 20% gap reduction gives a 25% capacitance rise. Also ignoring cable and stray capacitance, which add to C and reduce accuracy.
chapters.prereq: Electrostatics: C = Q/V and the parallel-plate capacitor; Unit 1 resolution and linearity.
chapters.leave: Bridge and charge amplifier circuits to Unit 6; microphone and pressure sensor construction to 3.7; MEMS capacitive sensors to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A capacitor microphone and a capacitive pressure sensor both work by a pressure-driven diaphragm changing the gap of a capacitor.
chapters.depth: Capacitor microphone: a thin metallised diaphragm and a fixed back plate form a capacitor; sound pressure moves the diaphragm; C changes; a charge amplifier converts the change to voltage; it needs a polarising voltage or an electret. Characteristics: flat response, high sensitivity, low noise and a high-impedance preamplifier. Capacitive pressure sensor: the diaphragm is one plate and a fixed plate or deposited electrode is the other; pressure deflects the diaphragm; C changes; signal conditioning gives the output; absolute, gauge and differential forms exist; used for low-pressure and differential measurements. Some syllabi call the microphone a condenser microphone.

figure.title: Capacitive microphone and pressure sensor
figure.aria: Block diagram: sound or pressure deflects a diaphragm, the gap and capacitance change, and a charge amplifier gives a voltage output.

chapters.example: A capacitor microphone has diaphragm area A = 25 mm², gap d = 20 μm, and εr = 1. Find C. A sound pressure moves the diaphragm by 0.020 μm. Find the new gap, the new C, and the percentage change in C.
chapters.trap: Connecting a capacitor microphone directly to a low-impedance amplifier. It needs a charge amplifier or very high input impedance, and cable capacitance changes sensitivity. For the pressure sensor, large diaphragm deflection makes C nonlinear.
chapters.leave: Charge amplifier and filter design to Unit 6; MEMS pressure sensors to Unit 5; acoustic sensor arrays to Unit 4.
